ui.writeNote: The 60 minutes are shared across all three tâches. Nothing stops you spending them all on one.
ui.nclcSub: The score bands IRCC uses to turn a TCF Canada result into an NCLC level, skill by skill.
ui.nclcNote: IRCC publishes these bands and can revise them. Check your own result against the current table on canada.ca before you file.

all.title: What prepfrancais gives you
all.sub: Practice material tells you what the exam asks. This tells you what your own answer would have scored.
all.b1: Every attempt comes back with a CEFR level and the score band it sits in, with the same caps the exam applies for length and off-topic answers.
all.b2: Prepositions, conjugation, agreement, spelling, anglicisms and the C1 turns of phrase you are missing — each highlighted in place with the correction and the reason for it.
all.b3: Corrections join a personal history and come back as spaced-repetition cards at 1, 3, 7 and 14 days, built from what you actually got wrong.

write.title: What the correction tells you
write.sub: Not a score out of twenty with no explanation — the level, the errors, and what a stronger version of your own text looks like.
write.t1: The word count, judged against the tâche
write.b1: 60–120, 120–150 or 120–180: the counter knows which tâche you are on and warns you before the grader caps your level for it.
write.b2: The same categories examiners penalise, tracked separately across attempts so you can see which one is actually costing you marks.
write.t3: A model answer at the target level
write.b3: The same consigne, answered at the level you are aiming for, so the gap between your text and a B2 one is something you can read rather than guess.

speak.title: What the evaluation gives you
speak.sub: Speaking is the section candidates practise least, because practising it alone usually means talking to nobody.
speak.b1: The preparation and speaking timers are the exam's, to the second, so two minutes thirty stops feeling like a suggestion.
speak.b2: What you actually said is transcribed, scored on the CEFR scale and marked up like a written answer — hesitations and repetitions included.
speak.b3: Tâche 2 needs somebody to question. The AI plays the examiner in role, so the one tâche you cannot rehearse alone becomes the one you can.

mcq.title: What the practice papers give you
mcq.sub: Full-length papers, in the exam's order of rising difficulty, marked the way the exam marks them.
mcq.b1: The score in your history is the score you got — nothing is computed in the browser, so a refresh cannot improve it.
mcq.b2: Every question comes back with the reasoning, including why the distractor you chose was built to look right.
mcq.b3: Practice mode marks each question as you answer it; test mode holds everything back until you hand in, on the exam's clock.

all.sub: Four steps, from your first attempt to a mistake you no longer make.
all.b1: One of the six official tâches, a theme, or a consigne you were given somewhere else and pasted in.
all.b2: The word ranges, the preparation times and the hand-in are the exam's, not approximations of them.
all.b3: A CEFR level, the score band, and every error highlighted where you made it with the reason for it.
all.b4: Your errors become cards and quizzes, spaced over the next fortnight so they are still there when you sit the exam.

write.sub: Four steps, from a blank page to a text you would be happy to hand in.
write.t1: Choose the tâche or the theme
write.b1: Pick one of the three written tâches, filter by theme, or paste the consigne you actually have to answer.
write.b2: The counter shows where you are against that tâche's minimum and maximum while you type, not after you submit.
write.b3: Errors in place, sorted by category, with a model answer at the target level beside your own.
write.b4: Repeat detection surfaces the four or five mistakes you keep making, which is where a level actually moves.

speak.sub: Four steps, from the first recording to one you would be happy for an examiner to hear.
speak.b1: One of the three spoken tâches, on its own or as a full twelve-minute sitting in exam order.
speak.b2: The preparation clock runs, then the recording starts. Neither waits for you, exactly as on the day.
speak.b3: What you said, written down and corrected — the fillers, the repetitions and the tense you dropped all become visible.
speak.b4: The second take of the same tâche, right after reading the correction, is where a speaking mark actually improves.

mcq.sub: Four steps, from a cold paper to a score you can rely on.
mcq.b1: Full-length papers at the exam's question count, ordered from easiest to hardest the way the exam orders them.
mcq.b2: Practice marks each answer as you give it; test mode runs the clock and reveals nothing until you hand in.
mcq.b3: Not just the correct option — why it is correct, and what the other three were designed to catch.
mcq.b4: Every attempt is kept, so the number that matters — how you do in the last ten questions — becomes visible.

hub.title: TCF Canada: format, scores and practice
hub.desc: What the TCF Canada actually asks of you — 39 listening questions, 39 reading questions, three written tâches and three spoken ones — what each section scores, and where to practise every one of them with AI correction.
hub.card: The whole exam in one page: format, timings, scoring and where to start.
hub.h1: The TCF Canada, section by section —
hub.h1b: and how to be ready for each one
hub.sub: Four papers, a little under three hours, and one set of numbers that decides your immigration file. This page sets out exactly what each section asks, how it converts to the NCLC scale, and where to practise it.
hub.about1: The Test de connaissance du français pour le Canada is the French exam IRCC accepts for Express Entry, provincial nominee programmes and citizenship. It is the same four skills every time — listening, reading, writing and speaking — sat in one session or split across two days depending on the centre.
hub.about2: The two comprehension papers are multiple choice, marked automatically on a scale that tops out at 699. The two expression papers are marked by examiners out of 20. IRCC then converts each of the four results into an NCLC level separately — and it is usually the weakest of the four that decides what your file is worth.
hub.b1: Listening and reading are 39 questions each, in rising order of difficulty.
hub.b2: Writing is three tâches sharing one 60-minute timer; speaking is three tâches in about twelve minutes, face to face.
hub.b3: There is no pass mark. Your result is a level, and the level you need depends on the programme you are applying under.
hub.tipsSub: None of these are about your French. They are about how the exam is built, and they cost points every session.
hub.ctaTitle: Find your weakest section this week
hub.ctaBody: Three writing corrections and three speaking evaluations, free and without a card. Enough to know which paper is holding your file back.
hub.tip1: Treating all four sections as equally urgent. Your file is usually held down by one weak skill — find it with a mock paper before you spend a month on the wrong one.
hub.tip2: Writing past the word range. Tâche 3 accepts 120 to 180 words; well past it, the examiner marks what fits and the extra work earns nothing.
hub.tip3: Preparing tâche 2 of the speaking as a speech. It is the only tâche where you ask the questions, and a prepared monologue scores badly there.
hub.tip4: Practising without a clock. The comprehension papers are as much a pacing test as a language test — 39 reading questions in 60 minutes is 92 seconds each.
hub.q1: How long does the TCF Canada take?
hub.q3: How long is a TCF Canada result valid?
hub.q4: Can I retake only one section?
hub.q5: What is the difference between the TCF Canada and the TEF Canada?
hub.a1: About two hours and forty-five minutes of exam time: 35 minutes of listening, 60 of reading, 60 for the three written tâches and roughly 12 for the spoken ones. Centres add registration and briefing on top, so budget half a day.
hub.a2: No. Every section returns a level, and it is the programme you are applying under that sets the level you need — NCLC 7 in all four skills for most Express Entry candidates.
hub.a3: Two years from the date of the exam for immigration purposes. IRCC sets that rule and can change it, so check the current one on canada.ca before you file.
hub.a4: No. The TCF Canada is sat as a whole and you resit all four papers, which is why finding your weakest skill early matters more than polishing your strongest.
hub.a5: They are two different exams, both accepted by IRCC, with different formats and different scales. The TCF Canada scores comprehension out of 699 and expression out of 20; the TEF Canada uses its own. Pick one and prepare for its format specifically.

practice.title: TCF Canada practice: all four sections
practice.desc: Practise the TCF Canada online: three written tâches with instant AI correction, three spoken tâches recorded on the exam's timers, plus reading and listening papers marked with every answer explained.
practice.card: Where to practise each of the four sections, and what the correction gives back.
practice.h1b: corrects you, not just times you
practice.sub: Most practice material gives you a question and a model answer. This gives you a mark on your own answer: your text or your recording, graded on the CEFR scale, with every error explained where you made it.
practice.aboutTitle: Practice that marks your own work
practice.about1: Reading and listening can be practised from any question bank: the answer is right or it is not. Writing and speaking are where practice usually breaks down — you write four hundred words, nobody reads them, and you learn nothing about whether they would have reached NCLC 7.
practice.about2: That is the gap this fills. Every text you write and every answer you record comes back with a level, the score band it sits in, and each mistake highlighted with the correction and the reason for it. The comprehension papers are here too, marked on the server with every answer explained.
practice.b1: The word ranges and the timers are the exam's, not approximations of them.
practice.b2: Errors are sorted into the categories examiners penalise, and tracked across attempts.
practice.b3: Start with three free writing corrections and three free speaking evaluations — no card.
practice.tipsTitle: How to spend your practice time
practice.tipsSub: Four habits that separate candidates who improve from candidates who only accumulate attempts.
practice.ctaBody: Six free AI corrections across writing and speaking. No card, and your error history starts from the first one.
practice.tip1: Sit one full mock paper before you plan anything. A month spent on reading is wasted if speaking is what is capping your NCLC.
practice.tip2: Write to the range, not to the clock. A 148-word tâche 2 that took you 25 minutes teaches you more than 200 rushed words.
practice.tip3: Re-record. The second take of the same tâche, straight after reading the correction, is where the level actually moves.
practice.tip4: Read your own error history weekly. Most candidates make the same four mistakes for months — agreement, past participles, prepositions after verbs, anglicisms.
practice.q1: Is TCF Canada practice free here?
practice.q2: Do I need an account to practise?
practice.q3: Are the topics real exam topics?
practice.q4: Can I practise with my own topic?
practice.a1: The trial is: three writing corrections and three speaking evaluations, with no credit card. After that, corrections come from a one-time pack rather than a subscription.
practice.a2: You can read every tâche, theme and practice paper signed out. An account is what stores your corrections and your error history, which is the part that makes practice compound.
practice.a3: Recent topics reported by candidates are collected under Recent topics, each with a model answer at the target level. The practice tâches follow the official formats and constraints.
practice.a4: Yes. Paste the consigne you were given, write your answer against it, and it is corrected exactly like a built-in one.

mock.title: TCF Canada mock test online
mock.desc: Sit a TCF Canada mock test: 39 reading questions in 60 minutes and 39 listening questions in 35, marked on the server with the correct answer explained and your score kept in your history.
mock.card: Full-length comprehension papers, timed and marked, with every answer explained.
mock.sub: Two comprehension papers at the real length and the real pace: 39 questions in 60 minutes for reading, 39 in 35 for listening. Marked when you hand in, with the reasoning behind every answer you missed.
mock.aboutTitle: Why a full-length paper is different
mock.about1: Answering twenty questions well tells you about your French. Answering thirty-nine in a row, in rising order of difficulty, tells you about your exam. The last ten questions of the reading paper are where most candidates lose the points that decide their NCLC, and no ten-question drill rehearses that.
mock.about2: Both papers here run at full length. Practice mode marks each question as you answer it, which is the right mode while you are still learning the question types. Test mode holds everything back until you hand in — the mode to use once the exam is a month away.
mock.b1: Questions run in the exam's order: easiest first, hardest last.
mock.b2: Marked on the server, so the score in your history is the score you got.
mock.b3: Every answer comes with the reason it is correct, not just a tick.
mock.tipsTitle: How to sit a mock properly
mock.tipsSub: A mock you interrupt is a practice set. Four rules that keep it a mock.
mock.ctaTitle: Find out where you actually are
mock.ctaBody: One full paper, marked, in an hour. It is the cheapest way to stop guessing which section is holding you back.
mock.tip1: One sitting, no pauses. The whole point is what your accuracy does in the last ten minutes.
mock.tip2: Answer everything. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so a blank is a guaranteed zero and a guess is not.
mock.tip3: Watch the clock at question 20, not question 35. Reading allows about 92 seconds a question — past 30 minutes at halfway, start moving.
mock.tip4: Review the ones you got right by guessing. They are the questions that will not go your way next time.
mock.q1: How many questions are in the TCF Canada mock test?
mock.q3: Does the mock cover writing and speaking?
mock.q4: Does my mock score convert to an NCLC level?
mock.a1: Thirty-nine in reading and thirty-nine in listening, the same as the exam and in the same rising order of difficulty.
mock.a2: In test mode, yes — 60 minutes for reading and 35 for listening, handed in when the clock reaches zero. Practice mode leaves the clock off.
mock.a3: Those have their own sittings, because they are marked differently: the writing simulator runs the three tâches on one 60-minute timer, and the speaking exam runs the three spoken tâches on the exam's preparation and speaking clocks.
mock.a4: The comprehension papers score on the same scale IRCC converts, so a mock result tells you which NCLC band you are near. Treat it as an indication for your preparation, not as an official result.

sim.title: TCF Canada exam simulator
sim.desc: Sit the TCF Canada expression papers under exam conditions: three written tâches on one 60-minute timer with no spellcheck and no paste, and three spoken tâches on the official preparation and speaking clocks.
sim.card: The expression papers under exam conditions — real timers, no spellcheck, hand-in at zero.
sim.h1b: the clock, the constraints, the hand-in
sim.sub: Practice is forgiving and the exam is not. The simulator takes away everything you will not have on the day — the spellcheck, the pause, the second look — and runs the two expression sittings exactly as they run.
sim.about1: Almost every candidate writes better in practice than in the exam, and the reason is rarely the French. It is that practice has an undo, a spellchecker, a pause to look something up, and no consequence for spending fifty of the sixty minutes on the first tâche.
sim.about2: The simulator removes all four. You get the tâches in exam order, one shared 60-minute countdown for the written paper and an automatic hand-in at zero. The spoken sitting runs the same way: the preparation clock starts, then the recording starts, and neither waits for you.
sim.b1: Written: three tâches, one 60-minute countdown, automatic hand-in.
sim.b2: Spoken: two minutes with no preparation, then 2 + 3:30, then 2 + 2:30.
sim.b3: Corrected afterwards exactly like a practice attempt — level, score band, every error explained.
sim.tipsTitle: Getting the most from a simulated sitting
sim.tipsSub: Four things to decide before you press start, so the sitting tests what you want it to test.
sim.ctaTitle: Sit one before the real one
sim.ctaBody: One hour, three tâches, no spellcheck. Then a correction that tells you what it would have scored.
sim.tip1: Budget the hour before you begin: roughly 15, 20 and 25 minutes. Write the split down and hold to it even when tâche 1 is going well.
sim.tip2: Do tâche 3 second if argumentation is your weakness. The order is yours; only the timer is fixed.
sim.tip3: Leave the last five minutes for rereading. Agreement and past participles are the easy marks, and they are only visible on a reread.
sim.tip4: Sit it at the same time of day as your real exam. A nine o'clock paper is a different exercise from a nine o'clock evening one.
sim.q1: Does the simulator match the real TCF Canada?
sim.q3: What happens when the timer reaches zero?
sim.q4: Do I need a microphone for the speaking simulator?
sim.a1: It matches the constraints that change how you work: the number of tâches, their order, the word ranges, the shared hour, the preparation and speaking times and the hand-in at zero. It is a preparation tool, not the official exam, and its scores are estimates.
sim.a2: No, and that is the point. A simulator you can pause tells you what you can write with unlimited time, which you already know.
sim.a3: The paper is submitted as it stands and sent for correction, half-written tâche included — which is exactly what the exam would do with it.
sim.a4: Yes. The spoken sitting records you and transcribes what you said, so it needs microphone permission in your browser. Any built-in laptop or phone microphone is enough.
sim.vSub: The written paper shares one hour across three tâches; the spoken paper times each tâche separately, preparation included.
sim.v1: The writing timer is shared, not per tâche — spend forty minutes on tâche 1 and the other two have twenty between them.
sim.v2: At zero the paper is handed in as it stands. The exam has no grace period and neither does this.
sim.v3: Spellcheck and paste are disabled, because the exam gives you neither.

nclc7.title: TCF Canada scores for NCLC 7
nclc7.desc: The TCF Canada scores you need for NCLC 7: 458–502 in listening, 453–498 in reading and 10–11 out of 20 in both writing and speaking — with the full conversion table and how to close the gap.
nclc7.card: The exact score you need in each section, and what to do about the one that is short.
nclc7.sub: For most Express Entry candidates, NCLC 7 in all four skills is the threshold that unlocks the points. Here is the score that means NCLC 7 in each section — and what to do about whichever one is short.
nclc7.about1: NCLC — Niveaux de compétence linguistique canadiens — is the scale IRCC scores French on, and level 7 sits around the lower half of CEFR B2. It is not a single number: each of the four skills is converted separately, and your file is judged on all four.
nclc7.about2: That is the part candidates miss. Reaching NCLC 9 in reading does nothing for a file where speaking came back at NCLC 6. The four results do not average, and the weakest is what most programmes look at.
nclc7.b1: 458 in listening and 453 in reading are the floors — a single point under and the band drops.
nclc7.b2: Writing and speaking need 10 out of 20, marked by examiners rather than by a machine.
nclc7.b3: Every skill is converted on its own; there is no averaging across the four.
nclc7.tipsSub: Four moves, in the order they usually pay off, when one section is short.
nclc7.ctaTitle: Find out which skill is short
nclc7.ctaBody: Three writing corrections and three speaking evaluations, free. Each comes back with a CEFR level you can read against the table above.
nclc7.tip1: Find the short one first. A mock comprehension paper plus one corrected writing and one corrected speaking attempt is half a day, and it tells you where the whole month should go.
nclc7.tip2: If writing is short, it is usually tâche 3. The argumentative text carries the most weight and is the one people practise least.
nclc7.tip3: If speaking is short, record and re-record the same tâche. A 10 becomes an 11 through fluency and range, and both come from repetition rather than new vocabulary.
nclc7.tip4: If reading is short, the fix is pacing before it is vocabulary. Most lost points sit in the last ten questions, reached with eight minutes left.
nclc7.q1: What TCF Canada score is NCLC 7?
nclc7.q2: Do I need NCLC 7 in all four skills?
nclc7.q3: Is NCLC 7 the same as CLB 7?
nclc7.q4: How does NCLC 7 compare to CEFR B2?
nclc7.q5: How long does it take to go from NCLC 6 to 7?
nclc7.a1: Listening 458–502, reading 453–498, and 10–11 out of 20 in both writing and speaking. Above those bands is NCLC 8 or higher; a point below and the skill scores NCLC 6.
nclc7.a2: For the Express Entry language threshold, yes — the four are assessed separately and the weakest governs. Check the exact requirement for the programme you are applying under, as it varies.
nclc7.a3: Yes. CLB is the English name (Canadian Language Benchmarks) and NCLC the French one, for the same scale. French results are usually quoted in NCLC.
nclc7.a4: NCLC 7 sits around the lower half of B2. Corrections here return a CEFR level, which is why the conversion table matters: a solid B2 written answer is generally in NCLC 7–8 territory.
nclc7.a5: It depends entirely on which skill is short and why. A pacing problem in reading can move in weeks; a speaking score held down by fluency usually takes a couple of months of regular recorded practice.

speak.title: TCF Canada speaking: the three tâches
speak.desc: The TCF Canada expression orale explained: entretien dirigé (2 min), exercice en interaction (2 min prep + 3 min 30) and expression d'un point de vue (2 min prep + 2 min 30), with recorded practice and an AI evaluation of each.
speak.card: Twelve minutes, three tâches, one examiner — and how to rehearse each of them.
speak.h1b: that decide a quarter of your file
speak.sub: The speaking paper is the shortest of the four and the one candidates arrive least prepared for. Three tâches, face to face, no second attempt. Here is what each one asks and how to rehearse it against the real clock.
speak.about1: You sit with an examiner for about twelve minutes and work through three tâches in a fixed order. The first begins immediately, with no preparation at all. The second and third each give you two minutes with a sheet of paper before you start speaking.
speak.about2: The examiner is not there to help you. In tâche 2 they answer your questions and volunteer nothing; in tâche 3 they listen. What is marked is range, accuracy, fluency and how well the answer fits what was asked — not whether the content is true.
speak.b1: Tâche 1: two minutes, no preparation, about you.
speak.b2: Tâche 2: two minutes to prepare, three and a half to ask your questions.
speak.b3: Tâche 3: two minutes to prepare, two and a half to defend a position.
speak.tipsTitle: What the examiner is listening for
speak.tipsSub: Four things that move a speaking mark, none of which is knowing more words.
speak.ctaBody: Three free speaking evaluations, no card. Enough to hear the gap between what you meant and what came out.
speak.tip1: Filling the time. An answer that stops at ninety seconds of a two-minute tâche loses marks that no amount of vocabulary earns back.
speak.tip2: Connectors. D'abord, en revanche, cela dit, en fin de compte — they cost nothing to learn and they are what makes an answer sound structured.
speak.tip3: Self-correction. Catching your own gender or tense error out loud reads as control, not as weakness.
speak.tip4: Registre. Tâche 1 is conversational and tâche 3 is not. Using the same voice for all three flattens the mark.
speak.q1: How long is the TCF Canada speaking exam?
speak.q2: Can I take notes during the speaking exam?
speak.q3: How do I practise the interaction tâche alone?
speak.a1: About twelve minutes in total: two minutes for tâche 1, five and a half for tâche 2 including preparation, and four and a half for tâche 3 including preparation.
speak.a2: During the two minutes of preparation for tâches 2 and 3, yes — you are given paper. Tâche 1 has no preparation, so there is nothing to take notes from.
speak.a3: Tâche 2 needs somebody to question, so the app plays the examiner: it answers the questions you ask, in role, and the exchange is evaluated afterwards like any other attempt.
speak.a4: The real exam is recorded by the centre. Here your answer is recorded and transcribed so the evaluation can point at what you actually said, and both stay in your history.

write.title: TCF Canada writing: the three tâches
write.desc: The TCF Canada expression écrite explained: message court (60–120 words), article or letter (120–150) and argumentative text (120–180), all inside one 60-minute paper, with AI correction of every attempt.
write.card: One hour, three tâches, three different registres — and the word range for each.
write.sub: The written paper is not one exercise repeated three times. It moves from a short private message to a public article to an argumentative text, and each one is marked against a different set of expectations.
write.about1: Sixty minutes cover all three tâches and nothing enforces how you split them. The usual guidance — about fifteen, twenty and twenty-five minutes — reflects how much writing each one takes, not a rule the exam imposes.
write.about2: What does bind you is the word range. Under it the grader caps the level whatever the quality; well over it you have spent minutes the third tâche needed. Both are avoidable and both cost candidates points every session.
write.b1: Tâche 1: 60–120 words, a short message to someone you know.
write.b2: Tâche 2: 120–150 words, an article, blog post or letter for a public reader.
write.b3: Tâche 3: 120–180 words, two opposing views weighed, then your own.
write.tipsTitle: Where written marks are actually lost
write.tipsSub: Four patterns that show up in almost every uncorrected answer.
write.ctaBody: Three free writing corrections, no card. Every error highlighted, explained and kept for review.
write.tip1: Ignoring the consigne's constraints. If it names a recipient, a place and a reason, all three have to appear — a beautiful answer that drops one is marked down.
write.tip2: Writing tâche 3 as an opinion piece. It asks you to present both sides before taking one, and skipping the first half is the single most common tâche 3 error.
write.tip3: Running short. Fifty-five words on a 60–120 tâche caps your level regardless of how good the French is.
write.tip4: Never rereading. Agreement and past participles are the cheapest marks on the paper and they are invisible while you write.
write.q1: How long is the TCF Canada writing exam?
write.q2: How many words should I write?
write.q3: What happens if I write too few words?
write.q4: Is the writing marked by a person?
write.a1: Sixty minutes for all three tâches together. The paper does not time them separately, so the split is yours to manage.
write.a2: 60 to 120 for tâche 1, 120 to 150 for tâche 2 and 120 to 180 for tâche 3. The ranges are part of the instruction, not a suggestion.
write.a3: The answer is treated as incomplete against the tâche, which caps the level it can reach. Writing well under the minimum costs more than a handful of grammar errors would.
write.a4: In the exam, yes — trained examiners, out of 20. Here it is marked by an AI working from the same criteria, which is what makes a correction arrive in a minute rather than a month.

listen.title: TCF Canada listening practice
listen.desc: TCF Canada compréhension orale: 39 multiple-choice questions in 35 minutes, each clip played once. Practise full papers marked on the server, with the reasoning behind every answer.
listen.card: 39 questions, 35 minutes, one play per clip — and how to practise for that.
listen.sub: The listening paper punishes hesitation more than any other section: the clip plays once, and while you are still deciding on question 12, question 13 has already started. Practising it is as much about rhythm as comprehension.
listen.aboutTitle: Why listening scores lag behind the others
listen.about1: Most candidates who have studied French can read far above the level they can listen at. Reading gives you as long as you want on a sentence; the listening paper gives you one pass at natural speed, often with a Québécois accent you have rarely met.
listen.about2: The fix is volume and pacing rather than grammar. Full papers, sat end to end, teach you to let a missed question go — the single behaviour that stops one lost answer from becoming four.
listen.b1: 39 questions in 35 minutes: under a minute each, audio included.
listen.b2: Marked on the server, with the reasoning behind every correct answer.
listen.b3: Every attempt is kept in your history, so the pacing improvement becomes visible.
listen.tipsSub: Four habits that move a listening score faster than more vocabulary does.
listen.ctaBody: Thirty-nine questions, marked, with the reasoning behind every one you missed.
listen.tip1: Read the question before the clip starts. Knowing what is being asked halves what you need to catch.
listen.tip2: Never replay during a mock. Replaying teaches you to understand the clip; the exam asks you to understand it once.
listen.tip3: Listen to Radio-Canada, not to French courses. The exam's Quebec accents and everyday speed are the thing you are training for.
listen.tip4: Let a lost question go immediately. Chasing it is how candidates lose the next two as well.
listen.q1: How many questions are in the TCF Canada listening test?
listen.q4: Can I take notes during the listening paper?
listen.a1: Thirty-nine, in rising order of difficulty, over 35 minutes.
listen.a2: No. Each recording plays once, which is what makes pacing so much of the exercise.
listen.a3: A deliberate mix — Quebec French alongside European, African and Belgian speakers — because the exam tests comprehension of French, not of one region's French.
listen.a4: Yes, and you should — particularly on the longer documents at the end, where a name, a number or a date is often the answer.
listen.vTitle: What the paper throws at you
listen.vSub: Short exchanges first, then announcements, interviews and reports — getting longer and faster as the paper goes on.
listen.v1: Questions rise in difficulty: the first ten are short everyday exchanges, the last ten are extended documents.
listen.v2: Accents vary on purpose — Quebec French, European French, African and Belgian speakers all appear.
listen.v3: You cannot go back. A question left blank stays blank, so answering something always beats answering nothing.

read.title: TCF Canada reading practice
read.desc: TCF Canada compréhension écrite: 39 multiple-choice questions in 60 minutes, from short notices to long articles. Practise full papers marked on the server, with every answer explained.
read.card: 39 questions, 60 minutes, 92 seconds each — the pacing paper.
read.sub: The reading paper looks like the gentlest of the four and quietly costs candidates the most points. The texts get longer and the questions get subtler exactly as your remaining time runs out.
read.aboutTitle: A pacing exam wearing a comprehension exam's clothes
read.about1: Sixty minutes across thirty-nine questions averages ninety-two seconds each, but the paper is not flat. The first fifteen questions can be answered in half a minute; the last ten need three or four minutes each, because the texts are long and the questions turn on implication rather than fact.
read.about2: Candidates who run out of time almost always spent it at the front. Banking minutes on the easy questions is the whole strategy, and it is only learnable by sitting full-length papers with the clock running.
read.b1: Full-length papers, in the exam's order of rising difficulty.
read.b2: Practice mode marks as you go; test mode marks only at hand-in.
read.b3: Every answer explained, including the distractor that made the wrong one look right.
read.tipsTitle: How to gain twenty points on the reading paper
read.tipsSub: Four adjustments that cost nothing in vocabulary and pay out immediately.
read.ctaTitle: Sit a paper with the clock running
read.ctaBody: Thirty-nine questions, sixty minutes, marked with every answer explained.
read.tip1: Bank time early. Be at question 20 with more than half the hour left, or the last texts get read at a skim.
read.tip2: Read the questions before the long texts. On documents of that length, knowing what to look for is worth more than reading well.
read.tip3: Eliminate rather than choose. Two of the four options are usually removable on grammar or on scope alone.
read.tip4: Never leave a blank. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so an unanswered question is a discarded point.
read.q1: How many questions are in the TCF Canada reading test?
read.q3: Is there a penalty for wrong answers?
read.q4: How is the reading paper scored?
read.a1: Thirty-nine, over 60 minutes, ordered from easiest to hardest.
read.a2: Everything from signs, adverts and short messages at the start to press articles and opinion pieces at the end, all in authentic-style French.
read.a3: No. A wrong answer scores the same as a blank, so guessing on a question you cannot finish is strictly better than leaving it.
read.a4: On a scale of 342 to 699 points, which IRCC converts into an NCLC level — 453 to 498 is NCLC 7.
read.vSub: From a two-line notice to a full opinion article, with the question types changing as the texts grow.
read.v1: Early questions are literal: the answer is a phrase you can point to in the text.
read.v2: Later ones are inferential — tone, intention, and what the writer implies but does not say.
read.v3: The final documents are long enough that reading them twice is not an option at exam pace.

speak1.title: TCF Canada speaking tâche 1: entretien dirigé
speak1.desc: Tâche 1 of the TCF Canada speaking exam: a two-minute directed interview about you, with no preparation time. What the examiner asks, what is marked, and how to rehearse it.
speak1.card: Entretien dirigé: two minutes about yourself, with no preparation at all.
speak1.sub: The exam opens with the only tâche that gives you nothing to read and no paper to plan on. The examiner asks about your life, your work, your studies — and the clock is already running.
speak1.about1: The examiner opens the conversation and asks about you: where you are from, what you do, what you studied, your family, your plans in Canada. The questions are ordinary and the answers are not fact-checked. What matters is that you keep talking, in French, for two minutes.
speak1.about2: Because it comes first and unprepared, tâche 1 sets the tone the examiner carries into the rest of the sitting. It is also the most rehearsable tâche on the paper: the question pool is small, and every candidate is asked some version of the same five things.
speak1.b1: No preparation time — the clock starts with the first question.
speak1.b2: Questions cover you: origins, work, studies, family, plans.
speak1.b3: Two minutes of continuous speech is the real requirement.
speak1.tipsTitle: How to prepare a tâche you cannot prepare
speak1.tipsSub: The tâche gives you no preparation on the day, which is exactly why it rewards preparation beforehand.
speak1.ctaBody: Record tâche 1, get it transcribed and marked, then record it again. Three free evaluations to start.
speak1.tip1: Build five blocks — origins, work, studies, free time, why Canada — of about thirty seconds each. Almost any question maps onto one of them.
speak1.tip2: Answer in three sentences, not one. 'Je suis ingénieur' is a dead end; the fact, an example and a reason fills the time and shows range.
speak1.tip3: Prepare the follow-up, not just the answer. Examiners ask 'pourquoi ?' and 'depuis quand ?' more than anything else.
speak1.tip4: Do not recite. A memorised paragraph is audible, and it collapses the moment the examiner asks something adjacent to it.
speak1.q1: How long is tâche 1 of the TCF Canada speaking exam?
speak1.q2: What questions are asked in the entretien dirigé?
speak1.q3: Do my answers have to be true?
speak1.q4: Can I ask the examiner to repeat a question?
speak1.a1: Two minutes, and there is no preparation time before it.
speak1.a2: Personal ones: where you live, what you do for a living, what you studied, your family, your hobbies, and what you plan to do in Canada.
speak1.a3: No. The examiner is marking your French, not verifying your biography — though inventing a life you cannot discuss fluently makes the tâche harder, not easier.
speak1.a4: Yes, and doing it in good French — 'pourriez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît ?' — costs you nothing. Answering the wrong question does.

speak2.title: TCF Canada speaking tâche 2: exercice en interaction
speak2.desc: Tâche 2 of the TCF Canada speaking exam: two minutes of preparation, then three and a half minutes asking the examiner questions to obtain information. Format, marking, and how to rehearse it alone.
speak2.card: Exercice en interaction: the only tâche where you ask the questions.
speak2.sub: You are handed a situation — organising a trip, finding a flat, enrolling on a course — and two minutes to prepare. Then three and a half minutes in which the examiner answers, and volunteers nothing you do not ask for.
speak2.about1: The card gives you a scenario and a goal: you need information and the examiner is the person who has it. For three and a half minutes you lead — you open, you ask, you follow up, you close. The examiner answers what you ask and nothing more.
speak2.about2: This inversion is what makes tâche 2 the one candidates most often prepare wrongly. A memorised monologue scores badly here whatever its quality, because the tâche is not testing whether you can speak. It is testing whether you can conduct an exchange.
speak2.b1: Two minutes with the card and a sheet of paper before you start.
speak2.b2: Three and a half minutes of exchange, led by you.
speak2.b3: Five to eight real questions is the shape of a full answer.
speak2.tipsTitle: What separates a 10 from a 14 here
speak2.tipsSub: Four things about this tâche that are specific to it and to nothing else on the paper.
speak2.ctaTitle: Rehearse the exchange, not a speech
speak2.ctaBody: An AI examiner that answers what you ask, and an evaluation of how you asked it.
speak2.tip1: Write question openers in your two minutes, not answers. Est-ce que…, Pourriez-vous me dire…, Qu'est-ce qui…, Combien de temps…, Y a-t-il…
speak2.tip2: Vary the grammar of your questions. Six questions all opening with 'est-ce que' reads as one structure repeated, and range is being marked.
speak2.tip3: React before you continue. 'Ah, d'accord — et dans ce cas…' turns a list of questions into a conversation.
speak2.tip4: Close it. 'Je vous remercie, c'est tout ce dont j'avais besoin' inside the time is worth more than a seventh question started at 3:25.
speak2.q1: How long is tâche 2 of the TCF Canada speaking exam?
speak2.q2: What kind of situations come up?
speak2.q3: How many questions should I ask?
speak2.q4: How can I practise an interaction on my own?
speak2.a1: Five and a half minutes in total: two minutes of preparation and three and a half minutes of interaction.
speak2.a2: Everyday practical ones — renting a flat, signing up for a course, organising a trip, arranging a service. Nothing requires specialist knowledge.
speak2.a3: Enough to fill the time and cover the goal, which is usually five to eight with follow-ups. Running out of questions at two minutes is the most common way this tâche is lost.
speak2.a4: The app plays the examiner: it answers your questions in role, in French, so you can rehearse the exchange and have the whole thing evaluated afterwards.

speak3.title: TCF Canada speaking tâche 3: expression d'un point de vue
speak3.desc: Tâche 3 of the TCF Canada speaking exam: two minutes of preparation, then two and a half minutes defending a point of view on a given document. Structure, marking, and how to rehearse it.
speak3.card: Expression d'un point de vue: two and a half minutes of structured argument.
speak3.eyebrow: Tâche 3 — Expression d'un point de vue
speak3.h1b: to take a position and hold it
speak3.sub: The last tâche gives you a short document and two minutes to think. Then you speak alone, without interruption, and everything the examiner marks — structure, range, precision — has to appear in a hundred and fifty seconds.
speak3.about1: You are given a short text or a statement — a social question, a habit, a trend — and asked what you think. The examiner does not interrupt. Two and a half minutes is long enough that an unstructured answer visibly runs out of things to say at ninety seconds.
speak3.about2: The mark is not for having the right opinion; there is no right opinion. It is for the range of language you deploy, the accuracy you keep under pressure, and whether those two and a half minutes have a beginning, a middle and an end.
speak3.b1: Two minutes with the document and paper before you begin.
speak3.b2: Two and a half minutes uninterrupted, alone.
speak3.b3: One position, argued — not a survey of what people think.
speak3.tipsTitle: A structure that fills the time
speak3.tipsSub: Four rules that turn two and a half minutes from an ordeal into a shape you can rehearse.
speak3.ctaTitle: Rehearse the shape until it is automatic
speak3.ctaBody: Record tâche 3, read the transcript marked up, record it again. Three free evaluations to start.
speak3.tip1: Use the same skeleton every time: situate the question, give your position, two arguments with an example each, then close. Rehearsing the skeleton is what makes the content easy.
speak3.tip2: Spend your two minutes on examples, not on wording. You will find the words while speaking; you will not invent an example under pressure.
speak3.tip3: Concede something. 'Certes, on peut comprendre que… mais' is the single structure that most reliably lifts this tâche's mark.
speak3.tip4: Prepare a closing line and use it. Stopping cleanly at 2:20 reads far better than being cut off mid-sentence.
speak3.q1: How long is tâche 3 of the TCF Canada speaking exam?
speak3.q3: Can I use my notes while speaking?
speak3.q4: What if I run out of things to say?
speak3.a1: Four and a half minutes in total: two minutes to prepare and two and a half minutes to speak.
speak3.a2: General-interest questions — technology, work, the environment, education, everyday habits. Nothing needs specialist knowledge, and no opinion is marked as wrong.
speak3.a3: You can refer to them, but reading them aloud is obvious and costs you. Notes work best as five words that remind you of your plan.
speak3.a4: That is a structure problem rather than an ideas problem. A fixed skeleton — position, two arguments with examples, conclusion — reliably fills the time, which is why rehearsing the shape matters more than collecting arguments.

write1.title: TCF Canada writing tâche 1: message court
write1.desc: Tâche 1 of the TCF Canada writing exam: a short message of 60 to 120 words in about 15 minutes. What the consigne asks, the constraints that must appear, and instant AI correction.
write1.card: Message court: 60–120 words to someone you know, in about 15 minutes.
write1.h1: Sixty to a hundred and twenty words —
write1.h1b: and every constraint has to appear
write1.sub: The shortest tâche on the paper, and the one most often marked down for something other than French: an instruction quietly dropped. The consigne names a person, a purpose and usually two details, and all of them have to be there.
write1.aboutTitle: A short message with a checklist hidden in it
write1.about1: You write to someone you know — a friend, a colleague, a relative — to invite, to describe, to tell, to apologise or to ask. The register is personal, the format is a message or a short letter, and the length is 60 to 120 words.
write1.about2: What makes it deceptively easy is the consigne. It typically carries three or four requirements: who you are writing to, why, and two or three things you must mention. Every one that is missing costs marks the quality of the French cannot recover.
write1.b1: 60 to 120 words — under sixty caps the level whatever the quality.
write1.b2: Personal register: tu or vous as the consigne sets it, and consistently.
write1.b3: Every element the consigne names must appear in the message.
write1.tipsSub: This tâche is rarely won on style. It is lost on four things.
write1.ctaTitle: Write one and have it marked
write1.ctaBody: Three free corrections. Word count checked against the range, every error explained in place.
write1.tip1: Underline the consigne's requirements before writing, and tick them off afterwards. It takes thirty seconds and it is where the marks are.
write1.tip2: Open and close like a real message. A greeting and a sign-off are part of the format being assessed.
write1.tip3: Keep the register consistent. Starting with 'salut' and closing with 'veuillez agréer' is a visible error.
write1.tip4: Aim near a hundred words. Ninety-five gives you room to be complete without eating tâche 3's minutes.
write1.q1: How many words for TCF Canada writing tâche 1?
write1.q3: What kinds of messages are asked for?
write1.q4: Should I use tu or vous?
write1.a1: Between 60 and 120. Below sixty the answer is treated as incomplete and the level is capped.
write1.a2: About fifteen minutes of the shared hour. The paper does not enforce it, but spending longer takes the time tâche 3 needs.
write1.a3: An invitation, a description of a place or an event, a piece of news, an apology, a request — always to somebody you know personally.
write1.a4: Whichever the consigne implies from the relationship, and then the same one throughout. Switching mid-message is marked as an error.

write2.title: TCF Canada writing tâche 2: article, blog or letter
write2.desc: Tâche 2 of the TCF Canada writing exam: 120 to 150 words in about 20 minutes, recounting an experience for a public reader. Format, register, and AI correction of every attempt.
write2.card: Article, blog or letter: 120–150 words for a reader who does not know you.
write2.h1b: for someone who does not know you
write2.sub: The middle tâche moves you from a private message to a public one. Same French, different reader — and the register, the structure and the level of detail all have to move with it.
write2.aboutTitle: Writing for a reader you have never met
write2.about1: The consigne asks for an article, a blog post, a forum contribution or a formal letter, and it usually asks you to recount something you experienced and to say what you made of it. The reader is a stranger, so nothing can be assumed and the register cannot be familiar.
write2.about2: The narrative half is where most candidates are comfortable and the reflective half is where the marks are. An answer that tells the story and stops has done half the tâche; the examiner is waiting for what you concluded from it.
write2.b1: 120 to 150 words — a narrower window than the other two tâches.
write2.b2: Public register: neutral to formal, no 'tu', no shorthand.
write2.b3: Recount, then reflect. Both halves are being marked.
write2.tipsSub: Four moves that fit inside a hundred and fifty words.
write2.ctaTitle: Write a hundred and fifty words that count
write2.ctaBody: Three free corrections, with the word counter holding you to the range as you type.
write2.tip1: Give it a title if it is an article. It costs four words and it signals that you understood the format.
write2.tip2: Use past tenses deliberately. Passé composé for the events, imparfait for the background — the contrast is one of the clearest range signals you can give.
write2.tip3: Land the reflection in two sentences. 'Cette expérience m'a appris que…' is worth more than three more sentences of narrative.
write2.tip4: Mind the ceiling. 150 is only thirty words above the minimum, so plan before you write rather than trimming afterwards.
write2.q1: How many words for TCF Canada writing tâche 2?
write2.q4: Do I have to have really had the experience?
write2.a1: Between 120 and 150 — the tightest range on the paper, so it needs planning rather than editing.
write2.a2: Usually an article, a blog post, a forum message or a letter. The consigne names it, and writing a different one is marked down.
write2.a3: Neutral to formal. The reader is a stranger, so 'vous' where a reader is addressed, full sentences, and no familiar shorthand.
write2.a4: No. Invent freely — the examiner marks the French and the structure, not the biography. An invented experience you can describe precisely beats a real one you cannot.

write3.title: TCF Canada writing tâche 3: texte argumentatif
write3.desc: Tâche 3 of the TCF Canada writing exam: 120 to 180 words in about 25 minutes, weighing two opposing views before giving your own. Structure, common mistakes, and AI correction.
write3.card: Texte argumentatif: two opposing views, then yours, in 120–180 words.
write3.sub: The last tâche decides most written scores and is the one candidates practise least. It asks for both sides of a question before it asks for your own, and skipping the first half is the most common way it is lost.
write3.about1: You are given a debated question — screens and children, remote work, city versus countryside, tourism, technology — usually with two positions already sketched. The tâche asks you to present them fairly and then to say where you stand and why.
write3.about2: It is the most demanding tâche on the paper because it needs a structure and the connectors to signal it, inside 180 words. It is also the most rehearsable: the shape never changes, so once you own the skeleton, only the content moves.
write3.b1: 120 to 180 words — the widest range, and the most to fit into it.
write3.b2: Both positions, presented fairly, before your own appears.
write3.b3: Connectors are part of the mark: d'une part, en revanche, cependant, en somme.
write3.tipsTitle: The skeleton that works every time
write3.tipsSub: Four rules for a tâche whose shape is fixed even when its topic is not.
write3.ctaTitle: Own the skeleton before the exam
write3.ctaBody: Three free corrections. Write it, read what the AI marked, and write it again.
write3.tip1: Four paragraphs: the question, one side, the other side, your position. Roughly 25, 50, 50 and 50 words.
write3.tip2: Signal every turn. 'D'une part… d'autre part… pour ma part' does more for the mark than a rare adjective.
write3.tip3: Argue, do not list. One reason with one example beats three assertions with none.
write3.tip4: Never open with 'je pense que'. Your position belongs at the end, after both sides have been given their due.
write3.q1: How many words for TCF Canada writing tâche 3?
write3.q2: Do I have to present both sides?
write3.q4: Why is tâche 3 the one to practise most?
write3.a1: Between 120 and 180, in about twenty-five of the sixty minutes.
write3.a2: Yes. The consigne asks for the opposing views before your own, and an answer that goes straight to an opinion is marked as not having done the tâche.
write3.a3: General debates: technology, the environment, work, education, city life, consumption. No specialist knowledge is needed and no position is marked as wrong.
write3.a4: It is the longest, the most structured, and the one where the connectors and register that separate B2 from B1 actually show. It is also last, so a badly managed hour leaves it half-written.
